newsitem.title: USA: U.S. banks tighten consumer loan standards.
newsitem.headline: U.S. banks tighten consumer loan standards.

text.p: Banks are toughening their standards for lending to consumers because more Americans are willing to file for bankruptcy to get around paying the money back, the Federal Reserve said Monday.
"Banks are pulling back somewhat in their lending to consumers," the nation's central bank said after the latest survey of 55 big domestic banks and 23 foreign-owned banks.

Senior bank officers are polled every three months about changes in their lending practices to businesses and households. The previous survey in late May also showed that concern among bankers about rising consumer loan delinquencies had caused them to pinch lending.
"These results represent the first time since 1981 that two consecutive surveys have shown a net reduction in willingness to make consumer instalment loans," the Fed said.

By contrast, standards for making business loans were little changed overall since May. In fact, many banks were making it easier for companies to qualify for commercial and industrial loans, the survey indicated.

Economist Sung Won Sohn at Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis said credit cards were the key problem area from the banks' point of view. Delinquency rates on credit-card payments was at a 15-year high, he added.
"But if you look at such categories as home equity loans or consumer instalment loans for new-car purchases, the credit-loss experience is not that much different than in the past," Sohn said.
Nearly half the big banks tightened their standards for approving credit card applications and about one quarter made it harder to get an instalment loan that required monthly payments.
Big banks said they got tougher because they were being forced to write off more losses than they had anticipated when they were aggressively soliciting customers for their credit cards and loans.
"These banks attribute this development largely to a rise in bankruptcies with a shorter than usual intervening period of delinquency," the Fed said.
Sohn said it appeared that not only banks, but also consumers, were becoming more cautious as credit-card use was holding steady or declining slightly in recent months.

"Economic growth is likely to slow in the second half, in part because of weaker consumer spending resulting from more caution by lenders and consumers," Sohn said. He noted that would be helpful since it is hard to slow growth when unemployment is relatively low.

"The question is will it slow enough to head off inflation," Sohn said, adding that a slowdown in economic growth to a 2 percent to 2.5 percent annual rate "likely won't be enough to alleviate the concern."
